candidates.text:
To Yama, residing in his hermitage, seated comfortably, a master of the Vedas and Śāstras, / the sages approached and asked, their minds held in check. // YSS_1.1 //
The Sages:
Those who have committed great sins, and minor sinners as well, / by which vows they are purified—tell that to us, O great sage. // YSS_1.2 //
Yama:
Touched by the wind and sun during the day, by the stars and breezes at night, / or by the two twilights, water is always purifying. // YSS_1.3 //
In its natural state, not pervaded by any impure substance (*amedhya*), it is always pure; / whether in a vessel or on the ground, drinkable water is a purifier of men. // YSS_1.4 //
A twice-born who is touched by an impure substance, by night or by day, / should immediately bathe and touch fire; and at the two twilights, he is always pure. // YSS_1.4A //

A man bitten by beasts of prey, camels, horses, and the like, but not by humans, / becomes pure immediately by bathing, at twilight and during the night. // YSS_1.5 //
Having unknowingly eaten the food of an outcaste, or by chance the food of a Caṇḍāla, / one is purified in ten nights by a diet of barley gruel mixed with cow's urine. // YSS_1.6 //
Those who have fallen from their vows by threatening suicide by water, fire, or hanging; those who have lapsed from asceticism or a fast unto death; / those who have attempted suicide by poison, falling from a height, or fasting; and those who have attempted suicide with a weapon; // YSS_1.7 //
these nine are apostates, excluded from all religious duties. / They are purified by a *Cāndrāyaṇa* (a lunar penance regulated by the moon's phases), or by two *Taptakṛcchras* (a 'heated' penance involving hot substances). // YSS_1.8 //

Sinners who reside in both worlds, who have fallen into 'black and variegated' sins, / are purified by two *Aindava* vows (a type of lunar penance) and by giving a cow and a bull. // YSS_1.9 //
For cremating one killed by a cow or a Brahmin, or one who died by hanging, / and for cutting the noose of such a person, one should perform a *Sāṃtapana kṛcchra* (a penance involving a diet of cow products and kuśa-water). // YSS_1.10 //
One afflicted by worms born from wounds or by flies and the like should perform a yearly *kṛcchra* penance; / for deluded intercourse, one should perform a *Parāka* (a twelve-day fast). // YSS_1.11 //
For each single sin that is committed, the wise know a penance; / but when all sins converge, no penance is known. // YSS_1.12 //
When all sins converge, taking up the skull-bowl is prescribed; / that Kāpālika vow is considered its ultimate penance by the wise. // YSS_1.13 //

For those who eat the food of a Kāpālika, and likewise for those who have intercourse with their women, / a year-long *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed if done knowingly; if unknowingly, two *Aindava* vows. // YSS_1.14 //
For drinking *surā* (a type of liquor) or other intoxicating drink, or for eating beef, / one who has undergone the hardship of a *Taptakṛcchra* is purified by a fire-offering with muñja grass. // YSS_1.15 //
If, having resolved upon a penance, the performer should die before its completion, / he becomes pure on that very day, in this world and in the next. // YSS_1.16 //
As long as one member of an undivided family performs a penance, / the others, by touching him, become impure and reprehensible. // YSS_1.17 //
They may not dine with others, receive gifts, be studied with, or be married; / when that vow is completed, they are all purified and become heirs to the property. // YSS_1.18 //

One who is eighty years of age, or a child under sixteen, / as well as women and the sick, are eligible for half a penance. // YSS_1.19 //
For a child who is over four but under sixteen years of age, / a brother, father, or another kinsman should perform the penance. // YSS_1.20 //
For one younger than this, there is no offense and no sin; / there is no royal punishment for him, and no penance is required. // YSS_1.21 //
For killing a person of mixed-caste birth, one should perform a *Sāṃtapana kṛcchra*; / for killing a Sūta, an *Atikṛcchra* penance is prescribed, and the same for a *Kuṇḍa* or a *Golaka* (types of children born of adultery). // YSS_1.22 //
For killing women in general, one should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* vow; / for killing a cow, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or one born of a regular-order union, // YSS_1.23 //

and for dining with them, having intercourse with their women, or accepting gifts from them, / one should properly perform a year-long *kṛcchra* penance for purification. // YSS_1.23A //
One who causes the death of other living beings should give a gift according to his ability; / he should also always perform a *Prājāpatya* penance (a penance sacred to the Lord of Creatures); this is the established rule. // YSS_1.24 //
The four perpetrators of great sins, without distinction, / are purified by entering fire, or by bathing at the conclusion of a horse sacrifice. // YSS_1.25 //
But those who commit these sins in secret / are purified in the month of Māgha by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn while standing submerged in water. // YSS_1.26 //
For having intercourse with another's wife, a man, a eunuch, or with horses, goats, sheep, and other animals—/ but not with a cow—one should recite the Pāvamānī hymns for three days. // YSS_1.27 //

for eating or drinking with them, secretly associating with them even once, / or performing oral intercourse, one should perform a *Taptakṛcchra*. // YSS_1.32A //
Caṇḍālas and Mushtikas, and likewise those of mixed-caste birth; // YSS_1.32 B //
for eating with them, having intercourse with their women, or accepting gifts from them, / a year-long *kṛcchra* is prescribed if done knowingly; if unknowingly, an *Aindava* vow is prescribed. // YSS_1.33 //
Those whose family custom is said to include the drinking of liquor by their women, / and those born from the 'field' (wife) of a fallen man, are known as people without proper family conduct. // YSS_1.34 //
Those who are outside the four *varṇas* yet consider themselves Brahmins, / who are of mixed origin through generations, are to be carefully avoided. // YSS_1.35 //

One born from a fallen ascetic, and one born to a Brahmin woman from a Śūdra man— / both of these should be known as Caṇḍālas, as should one born from a woman of the same *gotra*. // YSS_1.36 //
A child born of adultery with a woman of the same caste is a *Kuṇḍa* if her husband is alive; / if the husband is dead, he is named a *Golaka*. Both are likewise devoid of caste status. // YSS_1.37 //
Children produced by twice-born men with the wives of other men, / whether of the same caste or not, are all known as *Kuṇḍas* and *Golakas*. // YSS_1.37A //
They are not said to be of their mother's caste, nor are they considered to be of their father's caste; / such sons are unmarriageable by the relatives of either the father or the mother. // YSS_1.38 //
Testimony given by those dependent on women, by royal associates, by the young and the very old, or by those oppressed by the king, is not valid evidence; / neither a legal reply nor a deed performed by them is considered valid. // YSS_1.39 //

A killer of a horse, a killer of a man, a feller of tended trees, / and those who are attached to another's wife—they are to be killed with a weapon and not receive a lesser punishment. // YSS_1.40 //
He who with malicious intent harms another's wife, children, and household, / or his field, grain, wealth, and person—the king should have him killed with blows from a club. // YSS_1.41 //
The perpetrator, the consenter, the advisor, the instigator, the retaliator, / the planner, the helper, and the accomplice living with him are all to be killed; a man must clear himself of suspicion. // YSS_1.42 //
If a dependent, refugee, or servant commits a crime, he is the perpetrator; / the one who enjoys the fruit offered by him is not to be punished, and the one who merely provided the food is also released. // YSS_1.43 //

Others and yet others, destroyed by greed, and from that, the high and the low, and also others and yet others. // YSS_1.44 //
At sacrifices, weddings, and festivals, whether for men of equal or unequal status, / in these cases, they say there is no fault for one who is engaged in preparing food for others. // YSS_1.45 //
One who gives a weapon, poison, or fire to another incurs sin for a month; / however, if the action is motivated by the pursuit of righteousness, wealth, or desire, and not by the wish to harm another, there is no fault. // YSS_1.46 //
He who, without malicious intent, takes a vehicle or an elephant from its owner and goes away, / in that case the experts say there is no sin; he is ritually pure, yet still subject to punishment. // YSS_1.47 //
A wife, daughter, a kinswoman, or a daughter-in-law, a brother, son, servant, or dependent— / whoever among them is tainted by a crime is to be punished by the king. The master, if not the perpetrator, is not punished; this is the law. // YSS_1.48 //

One who helps another by giving wealth, by employing him in work, or by fighting for him, / and who thus abides in that man's heart, should be known as a companion in happiness and sorrow. // YSS_1.49 //
If someone, un-instigated, kills a large wild animal, a bird, a domestic animal of the same or another species, / or a man or a woman, his master is not liable for the penalty. // YSS_1.50 //
Whatever caste is born from the classes of the twice-born, sinners are not to be punished for performing sacrifices and the like; / confined and bound during the offering of planets, snakes do not bite if they are not frightened by others. // YSS_1.51 //
The king, having made him pay the owner, he is to be released by his master upon payment of the value of the animal. // YSS_1.52 //

If, in legal disputes, cows and other animals die due to their own willfulness or carelessness, / those who know the law do not declare a fault in that case, nor a fine equivalent to the animal's value. // YSS_1.53 //
If cows are killed by wild, fanged animals, and they were not protected, / they do not declare a sin for the one who set a trap to prevent harm, but for the one whose hand held the weapon. // YSS_1.54 //
When one person is killed by many acting together, and it is not known by whose blow he died, / the killer among them, having been identified by divine ordeal, should be punished by those appointed by the king. // YSS_1.55 //
Sometimes a person, in the act of purifying his sin, gives up his life and dies sinless. // YSS_1.55A //
Some, having argued with counter-arguments and proofs, say this is the authority; / that sometimes a person whose life is at its end simply dies—this is sung by the Vedas and the sages who were consulted. // YSS_1.56 //

For killing a blue jay, a frog, a cat, an owl, or a crow, / a Brahmin shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*, and the same for a mongoose. // YSS_2.5 //
For killing a peacock, a swan, a Bhāsa bird, a hawk, or a cockerel, / one shall be fined thirty *paṇas*, and the same for a wild peacock. // YSS_2.6 //
A Brahmin who has abandoned his sacred fire, who has neglected his twilight prayers, / or who acts as a servant to a Śūdra, the king should banish from the kingdom. // YSS_2.7 //
A Brahmin who has given up his fire, who does not bathe, who does not recite mantras, / or who does not worship the sun at dawn and dusk by performing his twilight prayers, // YSS_2.8 //
who does not perform the daily sacrifices, who eats the food of a Śūdra, / or who lives by the sword, shall be fined one *paṇa* each day. // YSS_2.9 //

A Brahmin who casts his seed in Śūdra women, or who lusts after a Śūdra woman, / the king should confiscate all his property and brand his forehead with a vulva. // YSS_2.10 //
A vulva-mark, a liquor-mark, a *surā*-mark on the forehead; / for one who casts his seed on prostitutes, the king, having confiscated everything, [should do this]. // YSS_2.11 //
One who bathes at the wrong time, bathes during the day, eats another's food or his own [improperly], / such a man has lost his rites; his wealth is declared to belong to the king. // YSS_2.12 //
For a Brahmin who has abandoned the prescribed duties and partakes of a Śūdra's food, / the king should confiscate all his property annually and present it to those learned in the Veda. // YSS_2.13 //
Wearing a lower or upper garment improperly is a wrongful amercement; / for a woman doing the same, he should impose a double fine. // YSS_2.14 //

But no punishment is ordained for children, the blind, the sick, or the elderly. / A man who urinates on a public road incurs a fault. // YSS_2.15 //
Likewise, it is ordained that feces and vomit should not be on a path; / one who urinates while standing incurs a double fine. // YSS_2.16 //
Urinating while facing the eastern or western direction, / and likewise discharging feces, shall incur a double fine. // YSS_2.17 //
A thief, a slanderer, a perpetrator of violence, and a Brahmin cohabiting with a Śūdra woman (*vṛṣalīpati*), / and one who abandons his dependents—these five are known as thorns in the side of the village. // YSS_2.18 //
The king, having identified these thorns in his kingdom, should remove them; / for if not removed, they create a dark falsehood for the people. // YSS_2.19 //

A thief, nourished by his thievery, adorned with bloody garlands, / and wrapped in filth—the king shall have him killed. // YSS_2.20 //
Placing the mark of a dog's foot on his face, wrapping him in a donkey's skin, / mounting the slanderer on a donkey, the king should banish him after confiscating his stolen wealth. // YSS_2.21 //
The king should banish from the kingdom the violent man who breaks into houses, steals property, and makes it his own, / having him cast out by a Caṇḍāla. // YSS_2.22 //
For breaking a vow and possessing a liquor vessel, two things are bound to him; / with his heart smeared with excrement, the king should cast out the *vṛṣalīpati*. // YSS_2.23 //
With his body smeared with ashes and fumigated with the hair and bones of a corpse, / the king, having confiscated all his property, should banish from the kingdom the one who has abandoned his sacred fire. // YSS_2.24 //

Being fanned with the hair of a corpse, his head adorned with a garland of it, / the king should make the man who violates convention go naked. // YSS_2.25 //
A wretch of a Brahmin who has begotten a child on a Śūdra woman, / the king should make that man, guilty of the sin of contact, live outside the village. // YSS_2.26 //
He who, mixing with good men, makes such a man eat in the same row, / shall incur the first fine. // YSS_2.27 //
Wealth given improperly, and knowledge acquired by twice-borns and others, / all becomes fruitless through conversation with slanderous men. // YSS_2.28 //
One who reveals a flaw in or deceives regarding the property of gods or Brahmins / shall suffer bodily mutilation, and a Brahmin shall have all his wealth confiscated. // YSS_2.29 //

One who points out a flaw for thieves is called a thief himself; / having confiscated all his property, one should brand the mark of a dog's foot on his face. // YSS_2.30 //
A man knows by a sign one born at night from a [certain] mark; / likewise, having identified a speaker of falsehoods by his signs, the king should banish him. // YSS_2.31 //
Having punished a witness who speaks falsely in a dispute, the king / should prescribe a vow of twenty [days] for one who conceals sins. // YSS_2.32 //
One observing a vow, begging for alms, who eats without having offered to the fire, / shall receive a mouthful [of food] at the proper time, if he is not ill. // YSS_2.33 //
A man who does not rise to greet his teacher, father, brother, father-in-law, or the king / shall be made to pay a fine of three *paṇas*. // YSS_2.34 //

One who scatters sweepings from a funeral, filth, a skull, or chaff on a village path / shall be fined ..... *paṇas*. // YSS_2.41 //
A householder who lets out water from leftover food / shall incur a double fine, and the one who releases it shall be punished with a silver coin. // YSS_2.42 //
For killing a partridge during the day, a Brahmin shall be fined three *paṇas*; / for killing a hare, a tortoise, an iguana, or a ram, sixteen. // YSS_2.43 //
A Brahmin who sells milk, milk products, salt, or oil, / or lac, shall incur the middlemost fine. // YSS_2.44 //
A Brahmin who sells cakes, cooked food, meat, soma, bones, or honey, / or hides, shall incur the middlemost fine. // YSS_2.45 //
A superintendent of markets who uses false weights and measures, / shall be fined one *paṇa*, as shall the one who uses them to buy. // YSS_2.46 //

A Brahmin who begets a child on a Śūdra woman and then marries her, / shall be fined one thousand if it is her first delivery. // YSS_2.47 //
A Brahmin who eats the cooked food of a *vṛṣalīpati* / shall be fined fourteen *paṇas*; double that during a period of impurity after birth. // YSS_2.48 //
For eating at a *śrāddha* (ancestral rite) in his house, he shall be fined the same amount; / he shall incur the first amercement, especially if there is no valid reason. // YSS_2.49 //
One who eats at the house of a *vṛṣalīpati* during the Anvaṣṭakā or Aṣṭakā rites / shall be fined fourteen *paṇas*, and the same for eating at a monthly rite. // YSS_2.50 //
One who accepts the order of precedence for the Aṣṭakā rites from a Śūdra's house / shall be fined half of ninety-six, and the same for having previously eaten in that house. // YSS_2.51 //

For consuming forbidden things like liquor, a Brahmin shall be fined sixteen *paṇas*; / for pressed juices, double that; for fish, he shall be fined one hundred. // YSS_2.52 //
Thus, for these offenses, the fine should be doubled for Soma-drinkers; / for eating the flesh of donkeys, horses, pigs, and the like, one is considered fallen. // YSS_2.53 //
A twice-born who strikes his wife or dependent with wood, bone, horn, or stone, / shall be fined one thousand, and must also undergo a shaving of the head. // YSS_2.54 //
He who inflicts a wound with his fingernails on his wife's exposed limbs, / the perpetrator, or one who has it done with his own limbs, shall be liable for the first fine. // YSS_2.55 //
A twice-born who engages in oral sex with a woman, or makes her do so, / or who makes another do so, shall be fined the first amercement. // YSS_2.56 //

A Brahmin who excessively sells the Veda becomes fallen, / as does one who mounts a woman like a horse, or kisses her private parts. // YSS_2.57 //
A Brahmin who intentionally emits his seed shall be fined fifty *paṇas*; / for having intercourse with cows, he shall be fined one hundred. // YSS_2.58 //
For having intercourse in an unnatural orifice, one incurs the first amercement; / one incurs the middlemost fine for going into the yoni of a she-buffalo. // YSS_2.59 //
A man who goes into the yoni of a cow shall be fined one thousand; / thus the fines are doubled for those observing a vow. // YSS_2.60 //
To one who is weary on the road, one should give way, or offer shelter; / the giver of shelter gets the merit of a sacrifice, while the non-giver is without refuge. // YSS_2.61 //

A Brahmin who serves a Śūdra woman is considered lower than a Śūdra; / by the very act of intercourse with a Śūdra woman, he becomes fallen. // YSS_2.62 //
By the very act of intercourse with a Śūdra woman, a twice-born begets a child of her nature; / the mother of that Śūdra child is said to cause his fallen state. // YSS_2.63 //
Therefore, a Brahmin who casts his seed into a dark woman, whether for sacrificial or domestic purposes, / awaits the loss of his sacred fire. // YSS_2.64 //
Seeing offspring from a Śūdra woman, they fall into great misfortune; / a Vaiśya's wealth by policy .. if the twice-born himself does not. // YSS_2.65 //
A Brahmin who cohabits with a Śūdra woman will see his ancestors look upon / the beautiful tooth of a dog, even of impure ones. // YSS_2.66 //

Therefore, in *śrāddha* rites, a twice-born must certainly shun the *vṛṣalīpati* / and dogs, and then feed the Brahmins. // YSS_2.67 //
All food that is touched, seen, or mixed with that of a *vṛṣalīpati* / becomes inedible; this applies to cooked food. // YSS_2.68 //
Even a worthy twice-born who sits in the same row as unworthy, inauspicious men, / and the *vṛṣalīpati* in the mire, should forfeit his ripened harvest. // YSS_2.69 //
Food touched by a fee or by silver / can be purified by the wise, but if touched during a *śrāddha*, it is ruined. // YSS_2.70 //
A Brahmin touched by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya woman / can be purified by certain means, but not one who has gone to a Śūdra woman. // YSS_2.71 //
A king who tolerates a *vṛṣalīpati* in a village / is unworthy of receiving good things, and his own interests and the village's are forfeit. // YSS_2.72 //

The holy nurse of Apollo's youth—when, my heart, or at what time
will you sing of her, of Delos? Indeed all
the Cyclades, which lie in the sea the holiest of islands,
are rich in song; but Delos wishes to bear away the first prize
from the Muses, because she washed and swaddled Phoebus,
the lord of song, and first praised him as a god.
As the Muses hate the singer who does not sing of Pimpleia,
so Phoebus hates whoever forgets Delos.
To Delos now I shall apportion a share of my song, that Apollo
of Cynthus may praise me for caring for his beloved nurse.
Windswept she is, and barren—such as, beaten by the sea,
she is the haunt of gulls rather than the run of horses—
fixed fast in the deep; and the sea, rolling much about her,
wipes off upon her the great foam of the Icarian water.

Therefore the fishers who roam the brine made their dwelling there.
But it is no cause for blame that she be named among the first,
when, toward Ocean and toward Titanian Tethys,
the islands gather, and she ever walks before them as their leader.
Behind, following in her tracks, comes Phoenician Cyrnus,
not to be despised, and Macris of the Abantes, home of the Ellopians,
and lovely Sardo, and the isle upon which Cypris first
swam up out of the water, and which she keeps safe in return for her landing.
Those islands are strong, fenced round with sheltering towers;
but Delos has Apollo. What stouter rampart is there?
Walls and stones may fall beneath the blast
of Strymonian Boreas; but a god is forever unshaken.
Delos, dear, such a helper stands around about you.
But if too many songs circle round you,

with what shall I entwine you? What is it that pleases you to hear?
Is it how at the very first the great god, smiting the mountains
with his three-pronged blade, which the Telchines wrought for him,
made the islands in the sea, and heaved them all
up from their lowest foundations and rolled them into the deep?
And these he rooted firm from below in the depths,
that they might forget the mainland; but you no constraint pressed—
you sailed free upon the open seas, and your name
was Asterie of old, since you leapt into the deep abyss
fleeing from heaven the marriage of Zeus, like a star.
So long as golden Leto did not yet draw near you,
so long you were still Asterie, and not yet called Delos.
Often did sailors, coming from the yellow town
of Troezen toward Ephyra within the Saronic gulf,

look upon you; and returning back from Ephyra
some no longer saw you there, while you had run
beside the swift, narrow strait of resounding Euripus,
and that same day, refusing the water of the Chalcidian sea,
swam onward as far as the headland of Athenian Sunium,
or Chios, or the isle's nipple dripping with water,
Parthenia (for it was not yet Samos), where the nymphs,
the neighbouring Mycalessian nymphs of Ancaeus, gave you welcome.
And when you gave Apollo a ground for his birth,
in return the seafarers laid this name upon you,
because no longer unseen did you sail, but in the deep
waves of the Aegean set the roots of your feet.
Nor did you tremble at angry Hera; she upon all
the women in childbed who bore sons to Zeus
roared terribly, but on Leto beyond all the rest,

because she alone was destined to bear to Zeus
a son dearer than Ares.
Therefore she herself kept watch within the upper air,
raging mightily and unspeakably, and she barred Leto
worn with her pangs; and two warders she set
to keep watch over the earth: the one, on the mainland's floor
seated upon the high crest of Thracian Haemus,
furious Ares kept guard with his armour, and his two horses
were stabled by the seven-chambered cave of Boreas;
the other, a watcher over the broad islands,
the daughter of Thaumas sat, swooping down upon Mimas.
There they remained, threatening those cities to which
Leto turned, and turning them aside from receiving her.
Arcadia fled, and the holy mountain of Auge
fled, Parthenion, and behind them fled old Pheneus.
Fled all the land of Pelops that lies along the Isthmus,

save Aegialus and Argos; for upon those
paths she did not tread, since Inachus fell by lot to Hera.
Aonia too fled the one road, and there followed
Dirce and Strophie, holding the hand
of their black-pebbled father Ismenus; and far behind followed
Asopus heavy-kneed, since he had been smitten by the thunderbolt.
And the earth-born nymph Melie, whirled in the dance,
ceased from it, and her cheek grew pale,
gasping for her coeval oak, when she saw the foliage
of Helicon shaken. My goddesses, tell me, Muses,
is it true that the oaks were born when the Nymphs were?
The Nymphs rejoice when the rain makes the oaks grow;
the Nymphs again weep when leaves are no more upon the oaks.
At them Apollo, still in the womb, was terribly enraged,
and uttered no idle thing, threatening against Thebe:

"Thebe, why, wretched one, do you put to the test your coming doom?
Do not yet, do not force me against my will to prophesy.
Not yet do I care for the tripod-seat at Pytho,
nor has the great serpent yet died, but still that
dread-jawed beast, creeping up from Pleistus,
wreathes snowy Parnassus with its nine coils;
yet all the same I shall speak something sharper than from the laurel.
Flee onward: swift shall I overtake you, washing my bow
in blood. You have got for offspring the children of an evil-tongued
woman. You shall not be my dear nurse, nor shall Cithaeron
be; but of the pure, and to the pure, may I be the care."
So he spoke. And Leto, turning back, again withdrew.
But when the Achaean cities refused her
as she came—Helice, the consort of Poseidon,
and Bura, the ox-stall of Dexamenus, son of Oeceus—

she turned her feet back toward Thessaly; and Anaurus fled,
and great Larissa, and the Chironian heights,
and Peneus too fled, winding through Tempe.
Hera, even then your heart lay pitiless,
nor were you broken, nor did you have mercy, when, stretching out
both her arms in vain, Leto cried such words:
"Nymphs of Thessaly, daughters of the river, tell your father
to lull his great stream. Twine yourselves about his beard,
beseeching that the children of Zeus be born in his water.
Phthiotian Peneus, why do you now strive with the winds?
O father, you are not mounted upon a prize-racing horse.
Are your feet thus always swift, or only over me
do they run light, and have you been made to fly
suddenly today?" But he was deaf. "O my burden,
where shall I carry you? For my poor sinews have given out.

Pelion, O bridal-chamber of Philyra, but you remain,
remain, since even the beasts upon your mountains often
have laid down their untimely birth-pangs, the lionesses."
And Peneus answered her, letting fall his tears:
"Leto, Necessity is a great goddess. For I,
lady, do not refuse your pangs; I know of others too
who washed themselves of childbirth from my waters. But Hera
has threatened me with abundance. Look, what a watcher
keeps watch from the topmost mountain, who would easily
drag me up from my depths. What shall I devise? Or is it
sweet to you that Peneus should perish? Let the appointed day come;
I shall endure for your sake, even if I must run forever
with a thirsting ebb, drained of my streams,
and be called, alone among rivers, the most dishonoured.
Behold me. What more? Only call upon Eileithyia."

He spoke, and checked his great stream. But Ares
was about to lift up the topmost peaks of Pangaeus
and hurl them into his eddies and hide his channels;
from on high he thundered and struck his shield with the point
of his spear; and it rang out warlike; and the mountains of Ossa
trembled, and the Crannonian plain and the ill-blown
edges of Pindus, and all Thessaly danced
with fear; such was the echo that roared from his shield.
And as when, the Etnaean mountain smouldering with fire,
all the recesses shake when the giant beneath the earth
shifts upon the other shoulder of Briareus,
and the furnaces roar beneath the tongs of Hephaestus
together with the works, and dreadfully the fire-wrought cauldrons
and tripods, falling upon one another, ring out—
such then was the clang of his well-rounded shield.

Yet Peneus did not give ground again, but stood as before,
steadfast as at the first, and stayed his swift eddies,
until the daughter of Coeus called to him: "Be saved, and rejoice,
be saved; do not for my sake suffer harm in return
for this compassion; your kindness shall have its recompense."
She spoke, and after many toils came to the islands
in the sea; but they did not receive her as she came—
not the Echinades, which hold a sheltered anchorage for ships,
nor Corcyra, the most hospitable of all,
since Iris, hastening upon them from the heights of lofty Mimas,
turned them all aside; and they at her rebuke
fled in a body down whatever stream each chanced upon.
Then to ancient Cos, the Meropian island,
she came, the holy haunt of the heroine Chalciope.
But this word of her son held her back: "Do not, mother,

bear me here. I neither blame nor begrudge
the island, since it is rich and good for pasture, if any other is;
but there is owed to it from the Fates another god,
the highest race of the Saviours; beneath whose crown
shall come, not unwilling to be ruled by a Macedonian,
both the inland regions and those that sit amid the seas,
as far as where the West is, and whence the swift horses
carry the sun; and he shall know the ways of his father.
And one day a common struggle shall come upon us
later, when the Titans of a later age, raising
against the Greeks a barbarian sword and Celtic war,
shall rush from the uttermost West, like snowflakes
or equal in number to the stars, when they most
graze across the sky; and the strongholds
and the Crissaean plains and the mainlands
shall be hemmed in on every side, and they shall see the thick smoke

of a burning neighbour, and no longer by report only,
but already beside my temple shall they catch sight of the phalanxes
of the enemy, and already beside my tripods
the swords and the shameless belts and the hated
shields, which for the Galatians, that senseless tribe,
shall set up an evil road; of these some shall be my prize,
and others, by the Nile, having seen those who bore them
breathe out their lives in fire, shall lie there
as the prizes of a king who has accomplished many labours.
O Ptolemy that art to be, these prophecies I reveal to you.
Greatly shall you praise the seer yet in the womb
hereafter, for all your days. But you, mother, consider this:
there is, dimly seen in the water, a slight island,
wandering over the seas; its feet are not in one place,
but it floats upon the tide like an asphodel-stalk,

now where the South wind, now the East, wherever the sea carries it.
Bear me thither; for to her you shall come, since she is willing."
As he spoke thus, the other islands ran away across the sea;
but you, Asterie, lover of song, were coming down from Euboea
to look upon the encircling Cyclades—not long ago,
but still behind you trailed the seaweed of Geraestus.
. . .
. . . burning, since you were scorched round about by fire,
seeing her, poor wretch, weighed down by her pangs:
"Hera, do to me this that is dear to you; for I have not
kept your threats. Come, come over to me, Leto."
You spoke; and she ceased from her grievous, longed-for wandering,
and sat beside the stream of Inopus, which deepest
the earth sends forth at that time, when with full flood
the Nile comes down from the Ethiopian crag;

and she loosed her girdle, and leaned back upon her shoulders
against a palm-trunk, worn out by grievous
helplessness; and down through her flesh ran the sweat of the South.
And she said, gasping: "Why, child, do you weigh down your mother?
Here, dear, is your island, floating upon the sea.
Be born, be born, child, and come gently from the womb."
Heavy-hearted bride of Zeus, you were not, after all, to remain
long unaware; such a messenger ran to you,
and spoke, still gasping, and her words were mingled with fear:
"Honoured Hera, far foremost of goddesses,
I am yours, and yours are all things, and you sit as queen,
the lawful mistress of Olympus, and we fear no other
hand of a woman; but you, mistress, shall know the cause of your wrath.
Leto is loosing her girdle within an island.

All the rest loathed her and would not receive her;
but Asterie called her by name as she passed by—
Asterie, the evil sweepings of the sea; you know it yourself.
But, dear lady—for you have the power—defend, mistress, your slaves
who tread your soil at your command."
So she spoke, and sat down beneath the golden throne like a hound
of Artemis, which, when it ceases from the swift chase,
sits, the huntress, beside her feet, its ears
held straight up, ever ready to receive the goddess's call;
like to her the daughter of Thaumas sat beneath the throne.
And she never forgets her seat,
not even when sleep lays its forgetful wing upon her,
but there, against the very corner of the great throne,
bending her head a little aside, she sleeps slantwise.
Nor ever does she loose her girdle or her swift

running-shoes, lest her mistress should say some sudden word to her.
And she, grievously vexed, spoke out:
"So now, you reproaches of Zeus, may you marry
in secret and bear in hiding, not even where the wretched
hard-labouring grinding-women toil, but where the seals
of the sea bring forth, upon desolate reefs.
Yet against Asterie I bear no grudge for this
offence, nor is there any way I would do her displeasure,
much as I should—for very wickedly she favoured Leto;
rather I revere her exceedingly, because she did not
tread my bed, but chose the sea instead of Zeus."
So she spoke; and the swans, the singers of the god,
left Maeonian Pactolus and circled
seven times about Delos, and sang over the birth-pangs,
the birds of the Muses, the most tuneful of winged things;
whence the child afterward bound just so many strings

upon his lyre, as often as the swans had sung over his pangs.
An eighth time they sang no more; he leapt forth, and over a long time
the Delian nymphs, offspring of an ancient river,
sang the holy song of Eileithyia, and at once the brazen
sky echoed back the piercing ululation,
nor was Hera angry, since Zeus had taken away her wrath.
Golden then, Delos, did all your foundations become,
and golden flowed the round lake all day long,
and golden grew the leafage of the natal olive-shoot,
and with gold brimmed deep Inopus, winding along.
And you yourself took up the child from the golden ground,
and laid him in your bosom, and spoke such a word:
"O great one, of many altars, of many cities, bearing much,
you fertile mainlands and you islands dwelling round about:
such am I, hard to plough; yet from me

shall Apollo be called Delian, nor shall any other
of lands be loved so much by another god—
not Cerchnis by lord Poseidon of Lechaeum,
not the Cyllenian hill by Hermes, not Crete by Zeus—
as I by Apollo; and I shall be no longer a wanderer."
So you spoke; and he drew the sweet breast.
Therefore from that day the holiest of islands
are you called, the nurse of Apollo's youth; nor does Enyo
nor Hades nor the horses of Ares trample you;
but to you year by year the tithe-bearing firstfruits
are ever sent, and all the cities lead up their dances—
those toward the dawn and those toward the evening and those in the middle
who have set up their lots, and those who above the northern
shore have their dwellings, a most long-lived blood.
These first bring the stalk and the sacred sheaves

of the corn-ears; which the Pelasgians at Dodona,
coming out from afar, are the very first to receive,
those servants who lie on the ground, of the unsilent cauldron.
Next they come to the Holy City and the mountains of the Malian land;
from there they sail across to the good
Lelantian plain of the Abantes; and no longer long
is the voyage from Euboea, since your harbours are near.
First did Oupis and Loxo and blessed Hecaerge,
the daughters of Boreas, bring these from the yellow Arimaspians,
and the noblest then of the young men;
nor did they come back home again,
but they were happy in their lot, and never were they without glory.
Indeed the Delian maidens, when the sweet-sounding wedding-song
frightens the spirits of the girls, offer their coeval hair
to the maidens, and the boys their first harvest of down,

the young men, offering it to those youths.
Fragrant Asterie, around you and about you the islands
have made a ring, and as a chorus surround you;
nor silent nor noiseless does Hesperus of thick locks
look down upon you, but ever loud-resounding.
Some sing the strain of the Lycian old man,
which the seer Olen brought you from Xanthus;
and the women of the chorus beat with their feet the firm ground.
Then too with garlands is weighed down the holy image,
that famous one of ancient Cypris, which once Theseus
set up with the youths, when he sailed up from Crete.
They, having escaped the harsh bellowing and the savage son
of Pasiphae and the winding lair of the crooked labyrinth,
lady, around your altar, as the harping rose,
danced in a circle, and Theseus led the chorus.
Thence the ever-living sacred things of the sacred ship

the children of Cecrops send to Phoebus, the rigging of that ship.
Asterie of many altars, of many prayers, what sailor,
what merchant of the Aegean, ever passed you by in his running ship?
Not even though strong winds blow upon him,
and need brings the swiftest voyage, but they furl
their sails quickly, and do not go on their way again,
before they have danced round your great altar, smitten
with blows, and bitten the holy trunk of the olive,
twisting their hands behind them; sports which the Delian nymph
devised, things for laughter to the young Apollo.
O hearth of the islands, well-hearthed one, hail yourself,
and hail Apollo, and her whom Leto bore.

1. A stranger from Atarneus once put this question to Pittacus
of Mytilene, the son of Hyrrhadius:
"Old father, two marriages are courting me. The one bride
matches my own rank in both wealth and birth;
the other is above me. Which is the better? Come, advise me,
which of the two shall I lead to the wedding?"
So he spoke; and the old man, lifting his staff, an elder's weapon,
said, "Look there—those children will tell you the whole tale."
Now those children, whipping their swift tops along,
were spinning them in the broad crossroads.
"Follow in their tracks," he said. And the man drew near
to where they stood; and they were saying, "Drive the one that matches you."
Hearing this, the stranger held back from grasping
at the greater house, taking to heart the children's omen,

and led the lesser bride home to his dwelling.
So you too, go your way and drive the one that matches you.
2. Someone told me of your death, Heraclitus, and it brought
a tear to my eye; and I remembered how often
the two of us sank the sun in talk together. But you, I suppose,
my Halicarnassian friend, are long since ash;
yet your nightingales live on, and on them Hades,
who carries off all things, shall never lay his hand.
3. [Sharp on every side about the tomb are thorns
and brambles; you will hurt your feet if you draw near.]
I, Timon the man-hater, dwell here. But pass on,
saying many curses if you will—only pass on.
4. Do not bid me rejoice, evil heart, but pass on.
For me it is the same joy that you do not laugh.
5. Timon—for you are no longer—which is hateful to you,

the dark or the light?
"The dark; for more of you are in Hades."
6. A shell am I, Lady of Zephyrium, of older days; but now you,
Cypris, hold me, the first offering of Selenaea,
a nautilus that sailed upon the seas: if there were winds,
spreading my sail from my own forestays;
but if Calm, that gleaming goddess, then rowing hard with my feet—
so my name accords with my work—
until I fell beside the shores of Iulis, that I might become
your far-seen plaything, Arsinoe;
nor any longer in my chambers, as before—for I am breathless—
let the egg of the dewy halcyon be hatched within me.
But grant your grace to the daughter of Cleinias; for she knows
how to do noble things, and she is from Aeolian Smyrna.
7. I am the labour of the Samian, who once received in his house
the divine singer; I sing of Eurytus, all that he suffered,

and of golden-haired Iole; and I am called a Homeric
writing. For Creophylus, dear Zeus, this is a great thing.
8. A boy was crowning the gravestone of his stepmother, a small stone,
thinking her life and her ways had changed with death;
but the stone fell and killed the boy as he bent over the tomb.
Flee, you stepsons, even the grave of a stepmother.
9. Theaetetus walked a pure road. And if that path of his
does not lead to your ivy, Bacchus,
heralds shall sound the names of others for a brief season,
but of him Hellas shall proclaim the wisdom forever.
10. Small, Dionysus, is the speech allotted
to the poet whose work goes well; he says only, in his longest, "I win,"
but the one on whom you do not breathe with favour—if anyone asks
"How did you fare?"—says, "Things go hard."

May this be the word for him who broods on unjust things;
but for me, my Lord, the brief and few-syllabled.
11. Here Saon, son of Dicon, of Acanthus, sleeps
a sacred sleep. Do not say that the good are dead.
12. If you seek Timarchus in Hades, to learn
something about the soul, or how you yourself will be again,
seek the son, of the tribe of Ptolemais, whose father
was Pausanias; you will find him among the pious.
13. The stranger was brief; therefore this verse too, which will say no long thing:
"Theris, son of Aristaeus, a Cretan"—and to me even that is long.
14. If you come to Cyzicus, it is little trouble to find Hippacus
and Didyme; for their family is in no way obscure.
And you will tell them a grievous word, yet say
this all the same: that here I hold Critias, their son.

15. "Is it under you that Charidas rests?" "If you mean the son
of Arimmas of Cyrene, he is under me."
"O Charidas, what is below?" "Deep darkness." "And the ways up?"
"A lie." "And Pluto?" "A tale." "We are undone."
"This is my true word to you; but if you want
the pleasant kind: a great ox in Hades costs a Pellaean penny."
16. Who knows well the daemon of tomorrow? When even you,
Charmis—you who were before our eyes but yesterday—
we buried, weeping, on the next day. Nothing more grievous
than this did your father Diophon ever see.
17. "Timonoe." "Who are you? By the gods, I should not have known you,
had not the name of your father Timotheus stood
upon the stone, and Methymna, your city." "Truly, I declare,
your widowed husband Euthymenes grieves greatly."
18. Crethis, full of tales, who knew how to play sweetly,

the daughters of Samos often seek—
their sweetest fellow-worker, ever full of chatter; but she sleeps
here the sleep that is owed to all.
19. Would that swift ships had never been! For then we
should not be mourning Sopolis, son of Diocleides.
But now his corpse drifts somewhere on the sea, and in his place
we pass by a name and an empty tomb.
20. Lycus the Naxian died not on land but on the sea,
and saw his ship and his life perish together,
when he was sailing, a merchant, from Aegina. He, a corpse,
is in the waters; and I, a tomb that holds only his name,
proclaim this wholly true word: "Avoid, O sailor,
putting to sea with the Kids when they are setting."
21. Twelve years old, his father Philippus laid the boy
here—his great hope—Nicoteles.
22. At dawn we were burying Melanippus; and as the sun

was setting, the maiden Basilo died
by her own hand; for to live, having set her brother on the pyre,
she could not bear. And the house looked upon a twofold evil,
the house of their father Aristippus; and all Cyrene
bowed its head, seeing the home of fair children left desolate.
23. Whoever you are that carry your foot past my tomb, know
that I am the son and the father of Callimachus of Cyrene.
You would know them both: the one once led
his country's arms; the other sang songs stronger than envy.
No cause for resentment: those children whom the Muses have looked upon
with no sidelong eye, they do not, when grey, cast off as friends.
24. Astacides the Cretan, the goatherd, a Nymph carried off
from the mountain, and now Astacides is holy.
No more beneath the Dictaean oaks, no more of Daphnis

shall we shepherds sing, but ever of Astacides.
25. Saying "Farewell, O Sun," Cleombrotus of Ambracia
leapt from a high wall down into Hades,
having seen no evil worthy of death, but having read
one writing of Plato's, the one on the soul.
26. A hero, the warder of Eëtion of Amphipolis,
I am set up, small upon a small porch,
holding a coiled serpent and a single sword; angered
at a man of Epeus, he settled me here on foot as well.
27. Callignotus swore to Ionis that never would he
hold any friend, man or woman, dearer than her.
He swore; but they say truly that the oaths of lovers
do not enter the ears of the immortals.
And now he burns with love for a man; and of the poor
girl, as of the Megarians, there is no word nor reckoning.
28. I had from little means a scanty living, doing

nothing terrible, wronging no one. Dear Earth,
if I, Micylus, ever praised anything base, may you not lie
light upon me, nor you other powers that hold me.
29. Hesiod's is the song and the manner; not the last of singers,
no—but I fear the man of Soli has milked off
the sweetest of his verses. Hail, you slender
discourses, the strained vigil of Aratus.
30. I hate the cyclic poem, nor do I take pleasure
in the road that carries many this way and that;
I loathe too the much-courted darling, nor do I drink
from the public fountain; I am sick of all common things.
Lysanias, you are indeed fair, fair—but before Echo
can say it clearly, someone else says, "He belongs to another."
31. Pour, and again say "To Diocles!" Not even Achelous
perceives those sacred ladlefuls.
The boy is fair, Achelous, exceedingly fair; and if anyone

says he is not—may I alone know what is fair.
32. Thessalian Cleonicus, wretched, wretched, no, by the keen
sun, I did not know you. Poor man, what has become of you?
Bones you are, and only hair still left. Has my own
daemon seized you? Have you met a harsh dispensation of the god?
I know it: Euxitheos has carried you off, and you too, coming,
gazed upon the fair one, poor wretch, with both your eyes.
33. The hunter, Epicydes, on the mountains tracks every hare
and the prints of every doe,
trudging through frost and snow; but if someone says,
"Here, this beast is struck down," he will not take it.
Such too is my love: it knows how to chase what flees,
but flies past what lies ready in its path.
34. I know that my hands are empty, empty of wealth; but, Menippus,
do not, by the Graces, tell me my own dream.

I grieve, hearing this bitter word continually;
yes, dear friend, of all that comes from you, this is the least loving.
35. Artemis, to you Phileratis set up this image here;
do you accept it, lady, and keep her safe.
36. Me, lion-strangling, boar-slaying lord, a branch of oak—
who set me here? "Archinus." Which one? "The Cretan."
"I accept it."
37. Past the tomb of the son of Battus you carry your feet—of one who knew
both song well, and well how to laugh in season over wine.
38. Lyctian Menitas,
having spoken these words,
dedicated this bow:
"Here, I give you my horn
and quiver, Sarapis;
but the arrows the Hesperitae have."
39. Her gifts to Aphrodite,

Simon, who wanders the streets, set up—an image of herself,
and the girdle
that kissed her breasts, and the torch,
and the very thyrsus that the poor woman used to carry.
40. To Pylaean Demeter,
to whom that man of the Pelasgians,
Acrisius, built this temple—these gifts the man of Naucratis,
and to her daughter below,
Timodemus dedicated,
a tithe of his gains; for so indeed he had vowed.
41. Priestess of Demeter once was I, and again of the Cabiri,
sir, and thereafter of the Dindymene Mother;
I, the old woman, now dust, who in the [pains of Eleutho]
was the patroness of many young wives.
And two sons were born to me, and I closed my eyes in their
arms in a fair old age. Go your way rejoicing.

42. Half of my soul still breathes; the other half I know not
whether Love or Hades has seized—only it is vanished.
Has it gone off again to one of the boys? And yet I forbade them
often: "Young men, do not receive the runaway."
Go, someone, and search there; for there, I know, that stone-worthy
and ill-loving thing of mine is somewhere turning about.
43. If of my own will, Archinus, I came reveling, blame me ten thousand times;
but if I come unwilling, let the rashness be.
Strong wine and Love compelled me; of these the one
dragged me, the other would not let me leave off my rashness.
And coming, I did not shout out who I was or whose, but kissed
the doorpost. If that is a wrong, I do wrong.
44. The stranger had a wound, and it went unnoticed. How painfully—
did you see?—his breath came through his chest. He drew it up

the third time as he drank, and the roses, shedding their leaves
from the man's garlands, all fell to the ground.
He is well roasted by something great; by the gods, it is no random
guess I make—a thief, I have learned the tracks of a thief.
45. There is something, yes by Pan, that is hidden; there is, yes
by Dionysus, here a fire beneath the ash.
I am not confident; do not embrace me. Often a quiet river,
unnoticed, gnaws away a wall;
so now too I fear, Menexenus, lest this silent creeper
slip in upon me and cast me into love.
46. "You will be caught; flee round about, Menecrates," I said
on the twentieth of Panemos; and "On what day of Loios?"—"the tenth"—
the ox came under the yoke of its own will. Well done, my Hermes,
well done, mine! I make no complaint over the twenty days.

47. What a good charm Polyphemus discovered
for the lovesick! Yes, by Earth, the Cyclops was no fool.
The Muses, Philippus, make love grow lean.
Truly, wisdom is an all-healing medicine for everything.
This, I think, is the one good that hunger too holds, even among hardships:
it cuts away the disease of love for boys.
And to me it is granted to say without stint to Love:
"Here, boy, your wings are clipped, little child,
and not a crumb do we fear you; for the charms,
both of them, are at home for the cruel wound."
48. The salt-cellar, on which, eating frugal salt,
Eudemus escaped great storms of debts,
he dedicated to the Samothracian gods, saying that this, according to his vow,
O people, having been saved from the sea, he set up thus.
49. Asking for good learning when he gave me, Simon, the son of Miccus,

to the Muses; and they, like Glaucus,
gave a great gift in return for a small one. And I lie here
gaping wide, the double Samian, the tragic
Dionysus, listening to the boys; and they say,
"The lock is sacred"—that is my dream to me.
50. Say, stranger, that I, Pamphilus, am dedicated here as the witness
of the truly comic victory of Agoranax the Rhodian;
not wholly bitten by love, but half resembling
a roasted fig and the lamps of Isis.
51. The Phrygian Aeschra, good milk, in every good thing
Miccus, while she lived, tended in her old age;
and when she died he dedicated her to be seen by those to come—
how the old woman keeps the grace owed for her breasts.
52. Four are the Graces; for besides those three, one more
was lately fashioned, and still is moist with perfumes.

Blessed and conspicuous among all is Berenice,
without whom not even the Graces themselves are Graces.
53. Theocritus, who darkens what is fair—if he hates me,
hate him fourfold; but if he loves me, love him.
Yes, by fair-haired Ganymede, heavenly Zeus,
you too once loved—I say no more.
54. Again, Eileithyia, come at the call of Lycaenis,
bringing safe delivery from her pangs, with a good birth;
so that now, mistress, this offering for a girl, but next time
for a son, your fragrant temple may hold some other gift.
55. That you have your due, Asclepius, the debt that Aceson
owed by his vow for his wife Demodice,
know it; and if perchance you forget, and demand it again,
the tablet says it will furnish testimony.
56. To the Canopian god, Callistion, daughter of Critias,
dedicated me, a lamp rich with twenty nozzles,

having vowed it for her child Apellis; and looking into my light
you will say, "Hesperus, how have you fallen?"
57. Euaenetus, who set me up, says—for I myself
do not know it—that for his own victory
I am dedicated, a bronze cock, to the sons of Tyndareus.
I trust the son of Phaedrus, son of Philoxenides.
58. In the temple of Inachian Isis stands the child of Thales,
Aeschylis, by the vow of her mother Eirene.
59. "Who are you, shipwrecked stranger?" Leontichus found here
a corpse upon the shore, and heaped this tomb over it,
weeping for his own perilous life; for he himself
has no rest, but like a gull he travels the sea.
60. Happy that, mad in all else, the ancient Orestes
was not mad, Leucaretes, with my madness,
nor put the Phocian to the test that proves
a friend; but if he had made even one play,

he would soon have lost his comrade by doing this—
and I no longer have many Pyladeses such as those of old.
61. You who pass by the tomb of Cimon of Elis,
know, as you pass, that you pass the son of Hippaeus.
62. Aenian Menecrates, you too were here not for long;
what, best of strangers, brought you down?
Was it the same that took the Centaur? The sleep appointed
for me came on; and the poor wine bears the blame.
63. Cynthian goats, take heart; for the bow of Echemmas
the Cretan lies in Ortygia beside Artemis,
the bow with which he emptied your great mountain. But now he has ceased,
you goats, since the goddess has made a truce.
64. So may you sleep, Conopion, as you make me
lie down by these cold porches.
So may you sleep, most unjust one, as you lull your lover
to sleep, and have met not even pity in a dream.

THE ADIEU AND RECALL
TO LOVE.
Go, idle Boy! I quit thy pow'r;
Thy couch of many a thorn and flow'r;
Thy twanging bow, thine arrow keen,
Deceitful Beauty's timid mien;
The feign'd surprize, the roguish leer,
The tender smile, the thrilling tear,
Have now no pangs, no joys for me,
So fare thee well, for I am free!
Then flutter hence on wanton wing,
Or lave thee in yon lucid spring,
